name: Colin Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the extruder and the cutter at the brick works up on Quarry Lane. Clay comes in from the pit, gets mixed, and my machine squeezes it out in a long column that the wire cutter slices into bricks before they go to the dryers and the kiln. I watch the moisture, change the cutting wires, and shout for the fitter when the auger starts grinding. My dad worked at the same works for thirty years, on the kilns.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you can drive round town and point at houses built with our bricks. What wears me out is the dust, the cold in winter and the pay, which isn't what the bigger works down south pay. My fiancée Selin and I are getting married next summer, and the wedding's eating everything we've got. There's maybe two weeks' money in the bank, and that's if nothing breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted all that talk. At work we'd have a laugh about it. I'm not online much, maybe the odd comment on the town page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me, which is fine. But building's slow this year and the works cut a shift in October. That worries me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take every extra shift going and keep my head down. I'd cut out the Friday pint with the lads until after the wedding. I wouldn't bother with any of the AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but the money still keeps me up. Same worry as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The wedding's next summer. What happens if money gets tight before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the wedding gets smaller, simple as that. Selin's mum wants a big do, but we'd cut the guest list before we'd borrow. I'd rather marry Selin (his fiancée) in the church hall with forty people than start our marriage owing the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the brick works itself doing all right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. When house building slows, bricks slow, and they cut the late shift. If they cut another, I'm one of the younger ones, so I could be first out.

I'd make the odd comment on the **town page**.
think: I think AI changes **nothing** for me, which is fine.
I think the **shift cut** at the brick works worries me more.

Cut the **Friday pint** until after the wedding.
feel: **Relieved**, but the money worry still keeps me up.

fieldNote: Colin's pressure is the **wedding costs** plus a recent **shift cut**, not AI.
He'd **shrink the wedding** rather than borrow, a clear value.
He sees himself as **first out** if more shifts go, because he's younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should work hard and they'll be fine. At work I'd say the office lot need to worry, not us. I'd not post anything about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've seen the robot arms at the big works on the telly, stacking bricks onto kiln cars. If our owners can afford one, they'll buy one, and that's two of us gone. I'm average at the job, so I'm not the one they'd fight to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well. I'd talk to the pastor about whether the church knows of anything going in town. I'd save what I can, but there's nothing to save until after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, deep down. Like when you hear a noise in the auger and hope it isn't what you think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at the brick works in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office would get computers to do the orders and the delivery planning, and then the owners would look at the floor. The big brick works already has robot arms stacking kiln cars, and our owners only need one good year to buy them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'm not one for courses. My dad never did one and he worked till he retired.

I'd tell colleagues the **office** needs to worry, not us.
think: I think robot arms stacking **kiln cars** could cost two jobs.

fieldNote: Colin relies on **church and community** networks, not retraining.

He expects robots at the works and sees himself as **vulnerable**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster, and it's been forced on us by people who don't work with their hands. At work I'd say we need to stick together. I'd probably say something on the town page too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished at the works. The office goes in 2028 and by 2031 the robots do the extruder and the stacking. I've got no trade except this, no savings, and a new wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle about his building firm, because laying bricks might last a bit longer than making them. I'd cut everything, the car, the phone, all of it. I'd lean on family and church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's gone. No plan, no money, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028, robots in 2031. You'd be married by then. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, because we'd be married with a rented flat and maybe thinking about kids. I'd be newly married to Selin (his wife-to-be) with no savings and no trade, just as the robots learn to make bricks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family, my church and Selin's family. That's how it's always been with us. We look after our own.

I'd tell colleagues we need to **stick together**.
think: I think I'm **finished** at the works by 2031.
I think I'd have **no trade**, no savings and a new wife.
do: Ask my **uncle** about bricklaying at his building firm.

S2.quote: I'd be newly married to Selin (his wife-to-be) with no savings and no trade, just as the robots learn to make bricks.
fieldNote: Colin has **no plan** beyond family and church, which fits panicked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people should stop moaning and get on. At work I'd say stick together. I'd not post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it helps a bit. I'd have a few more years of wages and maybe save something after the wedding. But I'd still be out by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save after the wedding, maybe fifty a month. I'd talk to my uncle about bricklaying. I'd wait and see what the works actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, all the time. Like waiting for bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years to AGI, robots by 2034. Does the extra time help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd have time to save, and Selin could keep her job at the school canteen. Five more years of wages from the brick works would let Selin (his fiancée) and me save, but not enough for kids and a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Selin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll manage, like my parents did. I'd say it and I'd mean it, even if I wasn't sure.

I'd tell colleagues at the brick works to **stick together**.

I think I'd still be **out by 2034**.

S3.quote: Five more years of wages from the brick works would let Selin (his fiancée) and me save, but not enough for kids and a house.
fieldNote: The extra years mainly buy **wages**, not a new direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's not panic. At work I'd say keep your head down and work. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels like I've got time to get settled. Kids, maybe, and a bit of savings. But I'd still lose the job in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save after the wedding. I'd maybe talk to my uncle about bricklaying in a few years. I'd wait to see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, but the worry doesn't go away. It just goes quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. You'd be 39. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a bit of breathing room, enough to have a family first. Ten years at the brick works would give Selin (his fiancée) and me time to have our first child before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the bricklaying earlier, if my uncle would take me. But I'd still wait, probably. I'm not one for jumping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be newly married with nothing behind me. What would help is an apprenticeship that pays, so I can learn bricklaying while still earning. My dad made bricks for thirty years, and I always thought I'd be able to say the same.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people round here would turn to the church first, not the government. That matters.

headlineQuote: My dad made bricks for thirty years, and I always thought I'd be able to say the same.
portrait: Colin, 27, runs the **extruder and cutter** at a brick works and is marrying Selin next summer.
He's **traditional**, trusts family and church, and avoids courses and new tech.
He's worried even in AI Plateau because of a **shift cut** and wedding costs.
He goes from **anxious** to **panicked** in AGI by 2028, with no trade or savings to fall back on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be newly married with **nothing** behind him.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** in bricklaying so he can learn while earning.
